s: Part three.
Structured output.
By the end of this part, you'll know how to stop asking for the right shape and start enforcing it, what that enforcement costs, and what it can never do.
Let's start with a picture.
Ask someone to jot delivery details on a scrap of paper.
It usually comes back fine.
Occasionally, though, you get a friendly note at the top.
Or the date in a format your filing system can't read.
Or two numbers the wrong way round.
Now hand them a printed form, with a box for each field.
Those mistakes have nowhere to happen.
That's this part.
When output goes straight into a system of record, like a ledger or a database, "usually right" isn't good enough.
Think about it.
A reply that arrives wrapped in extra text one time in a hundred and fifty is a crash one time in a hundred and fifty.
So you stop asking for the right shape.
And you start enforcing it.
The format in question is JSON.
That stands for JavaScript Object Notation.
It's the structured text format most systems exchange data in.
Here's the technical headline.
Prompting for JSON yields JSON most of the time.
And "most of the time" is a parse error in production.
There are two enforcement mechanisms.
Let's take them in turn.
The first mechanism.
Tool use, with a forced tool.
You define a tool.
Say one called record_shipment.
Its input_schema is your extraction contract.
Then you force the model to call it, with the tool_choice setting.
The model's answer arrives as the input to that tool call.
And you read it straight from there.
No regular expressions.
No stripping of code fences.
The tool_choice setting has exactly four modes.
One at a time.
One.
Auto.
The model decides whether to call a tool.
It's the default when tools are present.
Two.
Any.
The model must call some tool, but you don't say which.
Three.
Tool, with a name.
The model must call that specific tool.
And four.
None.
It forbids tool calls.
It's the default when no tools are supplied.
Now, the classic failure.
Leaving it on auto for mandatory extraction.
Why is that a failure?
Auto permits the model to answer in prose, and skip your schema entirely.
That's the cause of intermittent parser crashes on unusual inputs.
Now a source disagreement.
You should hear this one on air.
The lesson sixteen deck prefers tool_choice "any" for forcing structured output.
The study notes prefer naming the one tool.
So how do you reconcile them?
With exactly one tool defined, the two behave the same today.
But naming the tool is the tighter contract.
Why?
Because "any" silently loosens the guarantee the moment someone adds a second tool.
And when is "any" the right choice?
When you have several tools, every valid outcome calls one of them, and you genuinely want the model to choose.
For example, routing an input into one of several typed handlers.
So on the exam, four rules.
First.
If only one forcing option is offered, it's the right answer.
Second.
If both are offered for a single-schema extraction, prefer naming the tool.
Third.
If the stem has several tools and the model must pick, "any" fits.
And fourth.
If the contract is exactly one call per input, you add a setting called disable_parallel_tool_use to the tool_choice object.
The second mechanism.
Structured Outputs.
Instead of constraining a tool's input, it constrains the model's response itself.
You set a request parameter called output_config.format.
You give it a type of json_schema, and your schema.
An earlier name, output_format, is still accepted during the transition.
It's an alias, not a separate feature.
Separately, you can set strict to true on a tool definition.
That enforces that tool's input_schema.
There's a documented ceiling of twenty strict tools per request.
And the two can be combined.
Enforcement has costs.
And the exam likes honesty about them.
One.
It injects extra instructions, and those bill as ordinary tokens.
Two.
The first request against a new schema pays a grammar compilation cost.
Three.
Compiled grammars are cached for about twenty-four hours.
The cache resets on structural changes to the schema or tool set.
Not on rewording a description.
And two incompatibilities matter.
First.
Enforced structured output can't be combined with citations.
That returns an error.
Second.
It's incompatible with prefilling.
Prefilling means starting the model's reply for it.
Prefilling is also, separately, unavailable on Claude four point six and later.
So the old trick of prefilling an opening curly brace to force JSON is retired.
And Structured Outputs is its documented replacement.
Now the idea that makes schemas honest.
Think about a paper form that refuses to be submitted until the order number box is filled.
What do people do when they don't have an order number?
They make one up.
And nobody can tell it from a real one.
A form that says "leave blank if you don't have one" gets honest blanks.
In schema terms, it works like this.
A required field that can't be null gives the model two choices.
Violate the schema, or invent a value.
It invents.
The fix?
Type genuinely optional fields as a union of string and null.
And keep them in the required list anyway.
Why both?
Required forces the model to address the field.
The null option gives it a truthful way to say the document is silent.
Then you add an array called fields_not_found, where the model names every field it set to null.
That redundancy is deliberate.
It makes absence a declared act, rather than a passive omission.
And it gives your validator a cheap consistency check.
Two more habits.
First.
Set additionalProperties to false on every object.
That stops the model inventing keys you didn't design.
Second.
Write field descriptions that forbid inference.
For example: "the document's own stated total, do not compute this by summing line items."
Next.
Which schema rules are actually enforced?
The supported slice is: type, properties, required, items, enum, const, anyOf, allOf, oneOf, additionalProperties set to false, and pattern.
Not enforced are the numeric and length bounds.
That's minimum, maximum, minLength and maxLength.
So what happens to those?
The official software development kits strip those keywords.
They fold their meaning into the field description as a hint.
And they check your original schema on the client side, after the response returns.
So a length bound is a soft hint plus an after-the-fact check.
Not a guarantee.
Where the allowed values can be listed, use an enum.
Because enum is enforced.
One more response-handling habit.
Before you parse anything, check the stop_reason.
Two documented cases return output that doesn't satisfy the schema.
First.
A stop_reason of max_tokens.
That means the output was cut off mid-structure.
Raise the token limit if truncation dominates.
Second.
A stop_reason of refusal.
That means a safety response replaced the format.
Send refusals to a separate exception queue, not the retry loop.
Because retrying a refusal usually reproduces it.
Quick recap before the questions.
Force the shape with a named tool or Structured Outputs.
Know the four tool_choice modes.
Give absence an honest null, and list it in fields_not_found.
Use enum where values can be listed.
And check stop_reason before you parse.
Right.
Four practice questions.
Question one.
Here's the scenario.
A shipping-document extractor asks for "JSON only."
About one reply in a hundred and fifty arrives in markdown code fences.
Or with a friendly preamble.
Or with a renamed key.
And the repair layer keeps growing.
Output goes straight into a system of record.
What removes this whole class of failure?
Take a second.
The answer.
Define an extraction tool whose input_schema is the contract.
Force the call with tool_choice.
And read its input.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: "return raw JSON only, no backticks, no preamble," in capital letters.
Why?
That's persuasion.
It's the same approach that's already failing.
Wrong: prefill an opening brace.
Why?
It's retired.
It's unavailable on Claude four point six and later, and incompatible with enforcement.
Wrong: a tolerant parser that strips fences and maps renamed keys.
Why?
It treats the symptom.
And it becomes repair logic you maintain forever.
Question two.
Here's the scenario.
A support agent extracts ticket fields through a forced tool call.
The field order_number is a required string.
When a customer never mentions an order, the agent fills in a plausible number from their history.
And refunds land on the wrong order.
The ticket system can already route tickets with a missing field to a person.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Type order_number as string or null.
Keep it required.
And list every null field in fields_not_found.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: remove the field from the required list.
That sounds gentle.
Why is it wrong?
It loses the presence guarantee.
An omitted field no longer tells you whether the model checked and found nothing, or just skipped it.
Wrong: add a pattern for the order-number format.
Why?
An invented number is correctly formatted.
A pattern checks shape, never origin.
Wrong: a retry that resends the same email.
Why?
That's pure resampling.
The email still contains no order number, so the model can only invent another.
Question three.
Here's the scenario.
It's about Claude Code running headless.
That means with no one at the keyboard.
It runs on every pull request.
The team passes the flag --output-format json.
They expect the model's answer to match their findings schema.
But the answer inside the result is often free text.
Findings must conform on every run.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Pass the findings schema with a different flag, --json-schema.
And read the answer from the structured_output field of the result.
Here's the plain version.
Choosing a padded envelope instead of a plain one changes how the letter arrives.
Not what the letter says.
If you need the letter written on a specific form, you send the form.
The --output-format flag is the envelope.
It chooses the shape of the command line tool's own wrapper document.
The options are text, json, or stream-json.
The --json-schema flag is the form.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: switch to stream-json.
Why?
That changes delivery, not conformance.
Wrong: a system prompt rule.
Why?
It's persuasion.
And the words "every run" rule it out.
Wrong: a tolerant parser.
Why?
It still fails when there's no JSON at all.
We touched this in the chapter on Claude Code configuration and continuous integration.
It's worth saying the four look-alike names once, together.
One. output_config.format.
That's the programming interface request parameter that constrains the answer.
Two. output_format.
That's its older alias.
Three. --output-format.
That's the command line flag choosing the wrapper shape.
And four. structured_output.
That's the field in the command line result where schema-conforming output lands.
Question four.
Here's the scenario.
A developer tool labels each pull request with a risk_level value.
Mostly it says low, medium or high.
But occasionally it says "moderate-high," or "med."
And the dashboard crashes on unknown values.
A colleague proposes a maximum length of six characters.
The team wants a guarantee, not a likelihood.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Replace the free string with an enum of exactly low, medium and high.
Think of T-shirt sizes.
Tick boxes for small, medium and large give you only those three.
A rule saying "write no more than one letter" still lets someone write X.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: maxLength.
Why?
It isn't enforced.
It's stripped and checked afterwards.
And "med" would pass it anyway.
Wrong: a description saying "must be one of."
Why?
That's guidance.
Wrong: examples showing only the three values.
Why?
They make them likely, not guaranteed.
Two contrasts to lock this in.
First.
Prompt instruction versus enforcement.
An instruction makes an outcome likely.
A forced tool call, or Structured Outputs, makes a malformed outcome impossible.
When a stem says "every time," "guarantee," or "written straight into a system of record," pick enforcement.
And prose output is still right when a human is the reader.
Second, and you'll need this one in part four.
A stricter schema versus a semantic check.
A stricter schema fixes shape problems.
Stray keys.
Unknown values.
Malformed dates.
It can't fix a value that is well formed and false.
A fabricated date is a perfectly good date.
So when the problem is truth, the answer is never a tighter pattern.
And the words in a question that should switch this part on.
"One in a hundred and fifty," or "occasionally."
That means enforce, don't persuade.
"Invents a plausible value when missing."
That means nullable and required.
"Every run," at the command line.
That means the --json-schema flag.
"A guarantee," with a list of allowed values.
That means enum.
That's part three.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
Force the shape with a tool call or Structured Outputs, give absence an honest null, and remember the schema polices shape, not truth.
Coming up in part four: validation, retry and feedback loops for extraction quality.
